'''Vladimir Valentinovich Alexandrov''' ({{langx|ru|Владимир Валентинович Александров}}; born 1938; disappeared 1985) was a [[Soviet people|Soviet]]/Russian [[physicist]] who created a mathematical model for the [[nuclear winter]] theory. He disappeared while at the Second International Conference of Nuclear Free Zones Local Authorities in [[Córdoba, Andalusia|Cordoba]], Spain on 31 March 1985 and his ultimate fate remains unknown, though speculation continues.<ref name="sciencedigest">Revkin, Andrew (1986). "A Cold War Climate Mystery Endures: the Vanishing of Vladimir Alexandrov", ''[[Science Digest]]'', July 1986. p38.</ref><ref name="pulitzercenter.org">[http://www.pulitzercenter.org/reporting/scientific-thaw-during-cold-war Scientific thaw during the cold war. Pulitzer center. 2 May 2016 Kit R. Roane]</ref> One of his last papers was ''Man and Biosphere'' published in 1985; it is said to have charted the moving trend in the science of nuclear winter.<ref>''Climate as a problem of physics.'' A S Monin and Yu A Shishkov 2000 Uspekhi Fizicheskikh Nauk and Russian Academy of Sciences Physics-Uspekhi, Volume 43, Number 4 {{doi|10.3367/UFNr.0170.200004d.0419}}</ref> It was co-authored with [[Nikita Moiseyev]] and A. M. Tarko.<ref>[http://www.ccas.ru/tarko/bibl_e.htm 1985 Moiseev N.N., Aleksandrov V.V., and Tarko A.M. Man and Biosphere. System Analysis Experience and Model Experiments. Moscow, Nauka, 272 pp. (in Russian).]</ref>

When questioned by journalists in 1986, his acquaintances in Madrid gave differing accounts of how much he resisted when being driven towards the Soviet embassy.<ref name="sciencedigest" />

In 2016 [[Andrew Revkin]] said, "He's almost assuredly dead. ...This wasn't just, you know, thumb-sucking [[climate science]]. It was in the middle of a war—a long [[Cold War]]—and there were bodies."<ref name="pulitzercenter.org"/>

==Research==
According to an [[FBI]] white paper, Alexandrov was a mathematician specializing in [[computer science]]. In 1976 he was directed to shift his research from [[gas dynamics]] and [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] mechanics to [[climatology]]. In late 1970 he was assigned to the laboratory of [[computational physics]] in climatology at the [[Dorodnicyn Computing Centre]], working with Professor [[Nikita Moiseyev]] and A. M. Tarko. He was sent to the USA under a research exchange agreement, and studied at the [[NCAR]] in 1978, 1980 and 1982, which gave him access to the [[Cray-1]] supercomputer. In 1983 he was directed by [[Evgeny Velikhov]] to work on nuclear winter scenarios, heading an ad hoc group of 20 scientists.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160828155800/https://www.cia.gov/library/readingroom/docs/DOC_0000284025.pdf Interagency Intelligence Assessment (1984): The Soviet Approach to Nuclear Winter, page 10-11]</ref>

A pioneer in [[global climate model]]ling, he presented a mathematical solution to [[baroclinicity]] in 1982.<ref>Alexandrov, V. V. 1982. A general atmospheric circulation model with baroclinic arrangement. Rep. Acad. Sci. USSR 265(5):1094–1097.</ref> The following year, with G. L. Stenchikov, he used the model to calculate the consequences of [[nuclear war]]<ref>Alexandrov, V. V. and G. L. Stenchikov (1983): ''[http://climate.envsci.rutgers.edu/pdf/AleksandrovStenchikov.pdf On the modeling of the climatic consequences of the nuclear war] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229213544/http://climate.envsci.rutgers.edu/pdf/AleksandrovStenchikov.pdf |date=29 February 2024 }}'' The Proceeding of Applied Mathematics, 21 p., The Computing Centre of the AS USSR, Moscow.</ref> and the prospects of nuclear winter. However, [[Richard P. Turco]] and Starley L. Thompson, two major figures in the development of the nuclear winter scenario, described Alexandrov and Stenchikov's model as "a very weak piece of work" and "a primitive rendition of an obsolete US model".<ref name=badash>[https://books.google.com/books?id=y8M5vx-Lrk0C&q=badash+a+nuclear+winter%27s+tale Laurence Badash,  ''A Nuclear Winter's Tale'', Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 2009]</ref> Later they were to rescind these "harsh" criticisms and instead applauded Alexandrov's pioneering work, saying that the Soviet model shared the weaknesses of all the others.<ref>[http://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.31822020694212;view=1up;seq=11 An assessment of global atmospheric effects of a major nuclear war pg 59]</ref>

==Disappearance==
How Alexandrov disappeared and what happened to him afterward remains unknown,<ref name=badash/><ref>Vera Rich, "Nuclear winter expert vanishes without trace," ''Nature'', Vol. 316, 4 July 1985, 3 {{doi|10.1038/316003a0}}</ref><ref>Vera Rich, "Aleksandrov still not found," ''Nature'', Vol. 316, 8 August 1985, 479 {{doi|10.1038/316479b0}}</ref><ref>Tim Beardsley, "Soviet missing person," ''Nature'', Vol. 317, 19 September 1985, 191 {{doi|10.1038/317191b0}}</ref><ref>I. Andronov, "Where is Vladimir Aleksandrov?", ''Literaturnaya Gazeta'', n.30, 23 July 1986</ref> but several theories have been put forward. According to an article in the newsmagazine ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' in October 1985, the leading thoughts on the matter were that "The mystery of his disappearance had been compounded by the suspicions of some Western scientists that the nuclear winter scenario was promoted by Moscow to give antinuclear groups in the U.S. and Europe some fresh ammunition against America's arms buildup"...and that others "speculate that Alexandrov was planning to renounce the nuclear winter concept and may have been kidnapped by the KGB. According to another theory, the physicist defected to the West."<ref>[https://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,960025,00.html A 1985 ''Time'' magazine account of Alexandrov's disappearance. Also found in "Another Return From the Cold. By Jacob V. Lamar Jr. Sunday, June 24, 2001"]</ref>

A. Levakov suggests that his supercomputer work on nuclear winter was as embarrassing to the Soviet Union as it was to the USA.<ref name="daily.sec.ru">[http://daily.sec.ru/dailypblshow.cfm?rid=17&pid=10632&pos=9&stp=25 A. Levakov, "Supercomputer Technology and Projects in the U.S.", ''Jet Info online'', No.12 (115)/2002]{{in lang|ru}}</ref> According to the [[Mitrokhin Archive]], during a conference in 1987 the head of the [[KGB]]'s [[First Chief Directorate]] [[Vladimir Kryuchkov]] accused the [[CIA]]'s [[Deputy Director of the Central Intelligence Agency|Deputy Director]] [[Robert Gates]] of kidnapping Alexandrov and holding him against his will.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Andrew |first1=Christopher |last2=Mitrokhin |first2=Vasili |title=The Sword and the Shield The Mitrokhin Archive and the Secret History of the Kgb |date=1999 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=0-465-00312-5 |page=379}}</ref> [[Andrew Revkin]] assumes that he was a spy; it was never clear whether for the USSR, U.S., or both.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.edge.org/documents/schneider10/schneider10.html|title=Edge: STEPHEN H. SCHNEIDER 1945 – 2010|work=edge.org|access-date=15 July 2017|archive-date=6 December 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101206055320/https://www.edge.org/documents/schneider10/schneider10.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

US colleagues regarded his work on nuclear winter computer models to be on the extreme fringe, a position which toed the Soviet [[Party line (politics)|party line]] at the time – a position that, in private, he reportedly acknowledged was nonsense.<ref name="sciencedigest" />{{failed verification|date=May 2017}}
US colleagues also pointed to his unorthodox denial by the US visa agency to permit him access to dual-use [[supercomputer]]s, a denial which transpired after his name-dropping jokes about how he could freely access the coveted [[Cray X-MP]] at the US nuclear weapons lab [[LLNL]], and a denial which is likely a key factor in how he could have possibly fallen so far from favor in the Soviet establishment. Someone from Moscow would attempt to "phone"/internet access this powerful US computer a few months before his disappearance.<ref name="sciencedigest" />
 
Upon learning of the missing-person case that had not been reported on in Madrid at the time, nuclear winter colleagues, in particular the US team that included [[Alan Robock]], took a pact not to raise the alarm as they thought it conceivable that he had defected to the West. Robock would later regret taking this pledge as a lost opportunity to find him before the trail went cold.<ref name="sciencedigest" />
